purpose: Shows how ethical, legal and cultural frameworks were applied at each stage of the project, whose perspective each protects, and what each changed in the deliverables. Framework IDs refer to frameworks_verified.csv (all verified against official sources, 17 Oct 2026). Study IDs refer to the evidence base.

rows.stage: Methods: our own use of AI
rows.issue: AI tools assisted screening and extraction. Undisclosed or unchecked AI use would misrepresent the method and could breach integrity rules.
rows.frameworks: Australian Code for the Responsible Conduct of Research P1, P3, R21, R22 [8]; ACS Code 2.1 honesty [6]; Adelaide University Academic Integrity Policy (inappropriate use of AI) [11a]
rows.perspectives: Markers, client, future readers of the review
rows.effect_on_deliverables: Two independent AI screeners, blinded to each other, with a human adjudicator; every decision logged with a reason; agreement measured (kappa 0.79 to 0.88); AI assistance disclosed in the report. AI outputs were never presented as human work.

rows.issue: The project analyses data about real students (StudyChat, Hannover survey). Only the institution can decide whether this needs ethics review or is exempt.
rows.frameworks: National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research 2025, 5.1.15 to 5.1.17(a),(c) [7]; Adelaide University Human Research Ethics Procedure s3.4 to 3.5 [7]
rows.perspectives: Students whose data are in the datasets
rows.effect_on_deliverables: Only public, de-identified datasets were used, with no attempt to re-identify anyone. No primary data were collected (methodology decision M5). Raw student prompts are not quoted, because a few StudyChat prompts may contain residual personal details.
rows.status: Action: confirm the exemption position with the supervisor

rows.issue: Published papers and datasets carry copyright and licence terms. The EPFL data are CC BY-NC-ND, which bars sharing adapted versions.
rows.frameworks: Copyright Act 1968 s40, s41, moral rights [4a]; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 s2(a)(1)(B), s3(a) [4b]; CC BY 4.0 (StudyChat, Hannover)
rows.effect_on_deliverables: Findings are summarised in our own words, with very short quotes and full attribution. Only aggregate EPFL results are shared; our cleaned item-level EPFL file stays internal. All datasets and papers are cited.

rows.issue: Paid AI tools outperform free ones, so permitted AI use can favour students who can pay [S001], [R20], [R10].
rows.frameworks: HESF 2.2.1 equivalent opportunity [2]; AI Ethics Principles: fairness [5]; ACS Code 2.3.1(c) [6]
rows.effect_on_deliverables: D3 recommends allowing only AI tools every student can access, and the monitoring framework provides one university AI tool for everyone.

rows.stage: D2/D3: detection bias and cultural diversity
rows.issue: AI detectors are reported to be biased against non-native English writers [R15], [R28], and treating chat logs as proof can disadvantage multilingual students [S457].
rows.frameworks: TEQSA (2024) warning on detector false positives and bias [1b]; Adelaide University Academic Integrity principle 2 (fair, without bias) [11a]; HESF 6.4 preventing racism, from 2027 [2]
rows.perspectives: International students and students with English as an additional language
rows.effect_on_deliverables: No recommendation relies on AI detection. A flag or record is never treated as misconduct on its own; the live check decides. Legitimate language support stays permitted.

rows.issue: Vivas and live checks can measure anxiety or language rather than understanding [R81], [R51]. Assistive technology such as dictation produces unusual editing logs.
rows.frameworks: Disability Standards for Education 2005 (as amended 2025), 3.4, 3.5 [9]; HESF 2.2.1 [2]
rows.perspectives: Students with disability, anxiety or neurodivergence
rows.effect_on_deliverables: D3 includes accessible alternatives to orals, consultation on adjustments, reattempts and quieter rooms [R95]. The monitoring framework treats unusual editing patterns only as a prompt for a conversation, never as evidence of misconduct.

rows.issue: Capturing prompts, versions and keystrokes is collection of personal information. Which privacy regime applies to Adelaide University is uncertain.
rows.frameworks: Adelaide University Privacy Policy (APP-consistent practice) [3c]; Privacy Act 1988 and APPs where applicable, statutory privacy tort from 2025 [3a]; SA Information Privacy Principles Instruction, applicability unconfirmed [3b]; ACS Code 2.2(d) [6]; AI Ethics Principles: privacy [5]
rows.perspectives: All students; the University as data custodian
rows.effect_on_deliverables: Part C now requires a privacy impact assessment, a specific collection notice (the current policy covers metadata, not prompt or keystroke capture), data minimisation, a published retention period and access controls. The applicable regime is to be confirmed with the University privacy office.

rows.issue: Keystroke and prompt loggers are data surveillance devices under SA law, and the law applies to students as well as staff.
rows.frameworks: Surveillance Devices Act 2016 (SA) s3, s8 [13]; Adelaide University IT Acceptable Use Policy s3.6 [11b]
rows.effect_on_deliverables: Capture is limited to the University-controlled workspace, where the University's consent is likely to apply. Nothing is installed on a student's own device without their express consent. This is now a design constraint in Layer 1.

rows.stage: D2/D3: academic integrity and assessment standards
rows.issue: Assessment must confirm that learning outcomes are achieved and must uphold academic integrity.
rows.frameworks: HESF 1.4.3, 5.2.1 to 5.2.3 [2]; TEQSA principles 1 and 2 and propositions 3 and 5 [1a]; TEQSA (2025) secure task per unit [1c]; Adelaide University Assessment Procedure s6 (inform students about appropriate GenAI use) and s8 (certified assessment, interviews) [11b]
rows.perspectives: The University; employers relying on degrees
rows.effect_on_deliverables: D3 states the AI level in each task brief (matches s6), uses short live checks at key points (matches s8 and TEQSA's secure points) and routes misuse through the misconduct procedure, not through mark adjustments.

rows.issue: Students should know what is recorded and be able to challenge decisions based on it. Humans should stay the decision-makers.
rows.frameworks: AI Ethics Principles: transparency, contestability, human oversight [5]; DISR Guidance for AI Adoption (2025) [5]; UNESCO (2023) human agency [10]
rows.effect_on_deliverables: Students are told in plain language what is captured and why. Any concern from the record is raised in a live conversation where the student can explain. A person, not a system, makes every judgement.

rows.issue: Graduates will work where AI is routine; banning it would not prepare them. Clients want AI use and real understanding [D20], noting the questionnaire's framing [J5].
rows.frameworks: ACS Code of Professional Ethics 2023 [6]; TEQSA principle 1 [1a]
rows.effect_on_deliverables: D3 permits AI in most tasks and adds an outcome for critical and responsible AI use (LO5), assessed through captured interaction records.

rows.issue: The project used no Indigenous data, but a University capture system could collect data on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students.
rows.frameworks: CARE Principles [12a]; Maiam nayri Wingara principles [12b]; HESF 6.10 consultation, from 2027 [2]
rows.perspectives: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students and communities
rows.effect_on_deliverables: Part C notes that records must not be broken down by Indigenous status without Indigenous governance and consultation. Relevance to the current project is limited, and the report says so.

rows.issue: The client asked for AI detection, and the client's review of D2/D3 is still pending.
rows.frameworks: Australian Code for the Responsible Conduct of Research P1, R23 [8]; ACS Code 2.1 [6]
rows.effect_on_deliverables: The scope change explained why detection is unreliable and can harm students. The report states the evidence limits plainly, and client validation is recorded only once received.
